reason: A family of curves sharing one gradient function, with the constant c fixed by a point, shows why +c matters and how (2, 9) picks out one curve.

scenes.title: One gradient, many curves: the point picks $c$
scenes.purpose: See that integrating $6x-4x^{-2}$ gives a whole family of curves, and that the point $(2, 9)$ selects the one with $c=-5$.

elements.value: With $c = {c}$, the curve has $y = {14+c}$ at $x=2$. It needs to be $9$.

steps.text: After rewriting $\frac{4}{x^2}$ as $4x^{-2}$ and integrating, you get $y = 3x^2 + 4x^{-1} + c$. This is the M1 and first A1. Every value of $c$ gives a curve with the same gradient, just shifted up or down. Drag $c$ to see this.
With no $+c$ you are stuck on $c=0$, where the curve gives $y=14$ at $x=2$ and misses $(2, 9)$. The dashed gap shows how far off it is.
Put $x=2$, $y=9$ into $y$, not into the gradient: $9 = 12 + 2 + c$. So $c=-5$. Drag $c$ to $-5$ and the dashed gap closes. This is the final A1.
So $\mathrm{f}(x) = 3x^2 + \frac{4}{x} - 5$ is the only curve in the family through $(2, 9)$.

guide.what_you_see: The curve $y=3x^2+\frac{4}{x}+c$, which is the integral of the gradient $6x-\frac{4}{x^2}$ from the question, and the fixed point $(2, 9)$ that $C$ must pass through. A dashed segment at $x=2$ shows the vertical gap between the curve and that point.

legend.meaning: The curve $y=3x^2+\frac{4}{x}+c$ for the current value of $c$. Every choice of $c$ has the gradient $6x-\frac{4}{x^2}$, so the curves are vertical shifts of one another.
The point $(2, 9)$ given in the question, which $C$ must pass through.
The point on the curve $F$ where $x=2$, at height $14+c$. It moves up and down as $c$ changes.
The dashed segment from $P$ to $Q$. Its length is how far the curve misses $(2, 9)$.

interact.do: Drag the slider from $0$ down to $-5$, then try other values between $-15$ and $10$.
interact.watch: The whole curve slides up or down without changing shape, so its gradient at any $x$ is unchanged. At $c=0$, $Q$ sits at $y=14$, above $P$. As $c$ falls the dashed gap shrinks. At $c=-5$, $Q$ lands on $P$ and the gap vanishes.

question_link.text: The curve $F$ is the integral $3x^2+4x^{-1}+c$ of the gradient, after rewriting $\frac{4}{x^2}$ as $4x^{-2}$. That is the M1 and the first A1. Making $F$ pass through $P=(2, 9)$ means solving $9=12+2+c$, which gives $c=-5$ and $\mathrm{f}(x)=3x^2+\frac{4}{x}-5$, the final A1.

read_off: The on-screen note states the current $c$ and the height $14+c$ of the curve at $x=2$. You need this height to equal $9$, which happens only when $c=-5$.
